episodes.213972: Diurnally driven thunderstorm activity enhanced by an approaching upper low and fueled by abundant monsoonal moisture yielded heavy rain producing thunderstorms over the burn scars surrounding the Village of Ruidoso on the 20th. Flash flooding impacted areas just down stream of the Salt burn scar near Hollywood and Ruidoso Downs, and the South Fork burn scar north of Ruidoso near Alto. Late evening thunderstorms produced brief heavy rain that resulted in flash flooding in the town of Aztec, NM. The upper low continued toward the NM and AZ border on the 21st producing more rounds of afternoon and evening thunderstorm activity to areas along and west of the central mountain chain. A few of these thunderstorms produced heavy rain reaching up to 2 inches, resulting in considerable flash flooding impacts to Gallup and Zuni Pueblo. Heavy street flooding impacted travel across the area and also infiltrated the ground floor of Rehoboth McKinley Christian Hospital in Gallup, NM. Evacuations were ordered from severe flash flooding across portions of the Zuni Pueblo. The upper low migrated northward toward the Four Corners area and eastern UT, with abundant monsoonal moisture still funneling into western NM. This yielded another day of scattered to numerous afternoon thunderstorms along and west of the Continental Divide through western NM. These storms exacerbated ongoing flooding issues in Gallup and Zuni Pueblo, and producing isolated flooding impacts on the western edge of the Acoma Pueblo near the El Malpais Ranger Station.
episodes.214071: A line of thunderstorms moved south through Middle Tennessee late on July 21, 2026, and into the early morning hours of July 22nd. The primary hazard with these thunderstorms were very heavy rain which resulted in flash flooding. Many locations across Middle Tennessee received two to four inches of rain which fell very quickly. Numerous roadways were reported flooded and impassable with several water rescues having to be performed. In addition, these thunderstorms also produced strong wind gusts which caused multiple downed trees. Flash Flood Warnings were issued early for this event which gave an average lead time of 71 minutes.
episodes.214104: A front brought several rounds of showers and thunderstorms to southern New England in the afternoon and evening leading to ponding of water and sporadic flash flooding.

The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night. ||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. Severe thunderstorms downed trees and prompted power outages across southeast Ohio, particularly along and north of US-50, as well as in southern Lawrence County. ||Three tornadoes, two EF-2s and one EF-1, developed in Washington County and tracked east across the Ohio River into Pleasants and Tyler Counties in West Virginia. Heavy downpours also produced two to three inches of rain across parts of Perry, Morgan, Washington, and Athens Counties. This led to flash flooding, followed by rises on Duck Creek and the Little Muskingum. The system first lifted a warm front through the middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians on the night of July 20th into the early morning of the 21st, then steered a cold front east across the area late that evening into the night.||Showers and thunderstorms began to develop by late morning on the 21st, with a broken line of stronger storms progressing across the area during the afternoon and evening. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes ��� the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie ��� were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. episodes.214339: A cluster of strong thunderstorms, fueled by MLCAPE values between 500-1000 J/KG, materialized across Gila County during the late afternoon and early evening hours on the 20th. With DCAPE values between 1000-1500 J/KG, a surging outflow boundary emanating from this thunderstorm complex descended into the lower elevations of south-central AZ, including the Phoenix metro area, producing widespread 35-55 mph peak gusts based on surface observations. These wind gusts were enough to result in minor damage across portions of the Phoenix metro, including some downed trees and powerlines. At Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport, several cargo containers and a couple of airstairs causing minor engine damage to a couple of aircrafts were blown around by the strong winds.

episodes.214418: An inverted trough moving through eastern AZ combined with orographic lift provided the necessary forcing for ascent to spark the development of widespread deep convection across the eastern AZ high terrain, including Gila County during the afternoon hours on the 21st. Fueled by MLCAPE values between 1000-1500 J/KG and deep moisture with PWATs in excess of 1.5, strong thunderstorms developed across much of southern Gila County. Very light steering flow resulted in slow moving thunderstorm activity with very heavy rainfall in a short time span producing areas of flash flooding. In addition, a locally severe thunderstorm that developed near Globe, AZ produced a brief funnel cloud.

This event was notable for where the tornadoes occurred. For example, two tornadoes occurred in Pendleton County, WV--the first tornadoes in the county since 1998; one tracked for over 12 miles across multiple ridgelines.

episodes.216635: Scattered showers and storms developed over a large portion of central Virginia in the afternoon of July 21, persisting into the late overnight and early morning hours of July 22. Storms mainly produced damaging wind gusts and occurred  in association with an eastward-moving cold front over the Ohio Valley and a pre-frontal surface trough over the Mid-Atlantic. Additional shower and thunderstorm activity developed in the afternoon and evening hours of July 22, though this activity was more benign.
episodes.216646: Thunderstorms developed along and out ahead of an approaching cold front in two rounds. One in southeastern Ohio through northern West Virginia in the afternoon hours and then another in northwestern Pennsylvania in the early evening. The environment was potent for severe weather with 2000-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear of 40-50 knots, and notable curvature to hodographs with 100-200 m2/s2 of 0-1 km storm relative helicity. These parameters supported an all hazards day with supercells and line segments producing damaging wind, tornadoes, small hail, and flash flooding.
episodes.216647: Thunderstorms developed along and out ahead of an approaching cold front in two rounds. One in southeastern Ohio through northern West Virginia in the afternoon hours and then another in northwestern Pennsylvania in the early evening. The environment was potent for severe weather with 2000-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear of 40-50 knots, notable curvature to hodographs with 100-200 m2/s2 of 0-1 km storm relative helicity, and precipitable water values above the 95th percentile. These parameters supported an all hazards day with supercells and line segments producing damaging wind, tornadoes, small hail, and flash flooding.
episodes.216657: Scattered showers and storms developed over a large portion of central Virginia in the afternoon of July 21 and moved eastward toward the lower Maryland Eastern Shore in the late evening and early overnight hours. These storms occurred in association with an eastward-moving cold front over the Ohio Valley and a pre-frontal surface trough over the Mid-Atlantic. Two rounds of storms mainly produced isolated wind damage.
episodes.216658: Multiple rounds of showers and storms moved across central and eastern Virginia and the adjacent waters from the afternoon of July 21 through most of July 22. Gusty winds were observed across the Chesapeake Bay in association with this activity.
episodes.216659: Showers and storms produced heavy rainfall across portions of central and eastern Virginia from the afternoon and evening of July 21 into the early morning hours of July 22. This heavy rainfall led to isolated instances of flash flooding, particularly in urbanized areas.
episodes.216765: Tropical Storm Bertha moved slowly northwestward across the northeastern Gulf on July 21st while strengthening during the day. Increasing north-northeasterly vertical wind shear caused the low-level circulation to become displaced toward the northern edge of the deepest convection, with the strongest thunderstorms and winds concentrated mainly south and southeast of the center. As Bertha approached the north-central Gulf Coast during the evening, a thunderstorm within the stronger southern portion of the circulation produced a measured wind gust south of Venice.
episodes.217003: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 21st, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Ohio Valley along a cold front. The storms and the cold front pushed from northwest to southeast across southern Indiana and central Kentucky as an amplified mid- and upper-level trough pivoted across the eastern United States. Along and south of the cold front, a hot and humid environment was present, with temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s and dewpoint temperatures in the mid-to-upper 70s. The heat and humidity near the surface combined with cooling temperatures aloft resulted in a very unstable environment, with between 3500 and 4500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE observed. What made this setup uniquely potent was abnormally strong wind shear thanks to 40-50 knots of mid-level west-northwesterly flow. This resulted in well-organized, severe convection across the region, with a mixture of supercells, multicell clusters, and bowing segments observed across the area. While all severe hazard types were observed, damaging winds and tornadoes were the primary impact, with several swaths of straight-line wind damage and spin-up tornadoes observed. The most potent storm of the event was a supercell which tracked across Grayson, Hart, and Metcalfe County, producing three separate tornadoes, including a 21 mile-long EF-2 which went from Nolin River Lake to near the Hart and Barren County line. While storms moved at a fairly good clip to the southeast, precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches resulted in efficient rainfall production in some areas, with several instances of flash flooding observed across the area.
episodes.217082: A warm front lifting north through the region, followed by a cold front approaching from the west resulted in several thunderstorms developing across the region.
episodes.217192: Monsoonal driven isolated to scattered thunderstorms develop throughout the day on July 22nd, with several of these storms strong enough to produce small hail and breezy to gusty outflow winds. Storms in central Oregon produced brief, but strong outflow winds in the afternoon.
episodes.217228: A cold front pushed south across West Tennessee during the evening hours of July 21, 2026. The combination of modest height falls, 30-35 knots of deep-layer shear, MLCAPEs of 3500 J/kg, and precipitable water values well over 2 inches all provided support for storms along the front. Isolated wind damage occurred over West Tennessee.
episodes.217305: Another active monsoon day with flash flooding across Pima, Pinal and Cochise counties that led to multiple road closures across the area.
episodes.217356: Severe weather across Maine on July 22, 2026, was characterized by scattered afternoon convection tracking east out of New Hampshire into western and central Maine ahead of an approaching surface cold front.  The weak surface cold front and mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward through New England during peak afternoon heating. Boundary-layer moisture and surface heating yielded moderate surface-based instability.  Deep-layer shear was moderate, supporting isolated multicell clusters that brought a few areas of convective wind gusts that downed some trees.
episodes.217358: Severe weather in New Hampshire on July 22, 2026, was characterized by scattered afternoon convection tracking east out of Vermont ahead of an approaching surface cold front. The weak surface cold front and mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward through New England during peak afternoon heating. Boundary-layer moisture and surface heating yielded moderate surface-based instability. Deep-layer shear was moderate, supporting isolated multicell clusters that brought isolated areas of convective wind gusts that downed some trees.

NWS Storm Survey confirms an EF0 tornado west of Whitestown. A third tornado from a persistent, cyclic supercell developed southeast of Portersville and east of Interstate 79 along Yellow Creek Road. The tornado touched down at the end of a patch of woods on the west side of Yellow Creek Road resulting in large branches breaking and a large tree nearly entirely uprooted but still hanging on to the hillside with part of the root system intact. The tornado then progressed east through an open field and crossed Yellow Creek Road. On that side, sporadic tree damage was noted on a residential property with two large healthy trees fully uprooted and one landing partially on an outbuilding. Leaf and twig debris was scattered throughout the property. No additional|damage was found to the east beyond that property along Stone Church Road, through available road network was a limiting factor to evaluation within the wooded area between those two roads.

A tornado touched down on a farm in the 19300 block of Mechanicsville Road. Numerous trees on this property had their tops snapped off, with farm equipment (trailers and carts) tossed about. In the woods surrounding the property, a path of trees were snapped and uprooted in a convergent pattern. About 50 to 60 percent of the trees in the path were blown over. The tornado tracked through unpopulated woods and fields for about a mile before reaching another farm in the 19600 block of Cold Spring|Road. Here, additional trees were uprooted or snapped at the top.

KLWX radar indicated rotation co-located with a tornadic debris signature as the storm crossed this location.

The Buckhannon River near Buckhannon exceeded a flood stage of 23 feet on the night of July 21st. The river then rose to a crest of around 27.6 feet on the morning of the 22nd before falling back below flood stage that evening. Six feet of water near Weyerhaeuser was measured during this time, a car that floated down East Main Street, a submerged vehicle was observed near Lumber Street, and a home was impacted by flooding on Wimer Avenue.
